chapters.title: Chapter 2: How Each Component Is Taxed

lessons.title: Fully Taxable, Partly Exempt, Fully Exempt: The Three Buckets

children.text: Ishita and Aarav sit two desks apart at a Bengaluru bank. Same designation, same salary structure, same ₹16,58,400 of annual pay, same ₹30,000 monthly rent. Yet Ishita's taxable salary is ₹11,87,500 and Aarav's is ₹15,57,000.

The difference is not luck or a smart CA. It is which bucket each line of their payslip falls into, and which tax regime they chose. By the end of this lesson you will be able to sort any salary component into the right bucket in seconds.

body.text: Tax on salary is not charged on what you are paid. It is charged on what is left after every component has been sorted into its bucket.

children.text: First, three words people mix up
Exemption
: a component, or part of it, is kept out of your taxable salary altogether. HRA and gratuity exemptions work this way.

markDefs.definition: An amount of income that is excluded from taxable income altogether, usually subject to limits and conditions. Salary exemptions now sit under Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 10 of the 1961 Act).

children.text: Deduction
: the component is first counted as income, then a specified amount is subtracted. The standard deduction and employer NPS work this way.

markDefs.definition: An amount subtracted from your income after it has been added up. Examples include the standard deduction on salary and deductions like Section 123 (old 80C).

children.text: Perquisite
: a benefit in kind, like a company car or meal vouchers, whose taxable value is fixed by rules rather than by what it cost the employer.

markDefs.definition: A benefit in cash or kind provided by the employer, such as a company car, rent-free housing or meal vouchers. Its taxable value is set by rules under Section 17 of the Income-tax Act, 2025.

body.text: Why the distinction matters: the new tax regime under Section 202 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 115BAC of the 1961 Act) removes most exemptions and most deductions, but keeps a specific short list of each. So "is this taxable?" always has a second question attached: "in which regime?"

body.title: Bucket check
body.question: Deepak encashes 15 days of unused leave in March while continuing in his job. How is it taxed?
options: Fully exempt, leave encashment is always tax-free
Taxable only in the old regime
body.explanation: Leave encashed while you are still in service is fully taxable salary. The ₹25,00,000 exemption applies only to leave encashment received on retirement or resignation, and it is available in both regimes.

body.text: Professional tax is deducted from your salary in states like Karnataka, Maharashtra and West Bengal whichever regime you choose. But it reduces your taxable salary only in the old regime. In the new regime it is a pure cost.

children.text: Sorting Ishita's and Aarav's payslips

Both receive the same annual pay. Both pay ₹30,000 a month rent in Bengaluru and have two school-going children. Ishita has opted for the old regime and took a ₹40,000 domestic family trip on flight tickets. Aarav is on the default new regime.

body.caption: *Professional tax is subtracted only in the old regime.

children.text: Ishita, old regime
HRA exemption = least of: actual HRA ₹4,00,000; rent minus 10% of basic = ₹3,60,000 minus ₹80,000 = ₹2,80,000; 50% of basic (Bengaluru is now in the 50% list) = ₹4,00,000. So ₹2,80,000.
LTA exempt: actual air fare of ₹40,000 for a domestic trip, within the allowance.
Children education allowance exempt: ₹3,000 × 2 children × 12 months = ₹72,000.
Meal vouchers exempt: ₹100 per meal is within the ₹200 limit, so ₹26,400.
Salary after exemptions: ₹16,58,400 minus ₹4,18,400 = ₹12,40,000.
Less standard deduction ₹50,000 and professional tax ₹2,500: taxable salary ₹11,87,500.
Aarav, new regime
Only meal vouchers stay exempt: ₹26,400.
Salary after exemptions: ₹16,32,000.
Less standard deduction ₹75,000. No professional tax deduction: taxable salary ₹15,57,000.

body.text: Aarav's taxable salary is ₹3,69,500 higher. That does not automatically mean he pays more tax, because the new regime has lower slab rates and a ₹60,000 rebate, while Ishita also has to fund her Section 123 (old 80C) investments to get the most from the old regime. Taxable salary is only step one. The full regime comparison is covered in our Old Tax Regime vs New Tax Regime course.

children.text: Your turn

body.title: Neel's taxable salary
body.prompt: Neel, in the new regime, receives: basic ₹6,00,000, HRA ₹3,00,000, special allowance ₹2,40,000, meal vouchers ₹24,000 (within the per-meal limit) and children education allowance ₹36,000. He pays rent and has one child. What is his taxable salary?
body.explanation: Total pay = ₹12,00,000. In the new regime only the meal vouchers are exempt (₹24,000). HRA and children education allowance are fully taxable. Taxable salary = ₹12,00,000 minus ₹24,000 minus ₹75,000 standard deduction = ₹11,01,000. As a bonus, that is below ₹12,00,000, so the Section 156 rebate (old 87A) brings his tax to zero.

body.title: Farah's education allowance
body.prompt: Farah, in the old regime, has three children in school. Her employer pays children education allowance of ₹2,500 a month per child. How much of it is exempt for the year?
body.explanation: The exemption applies to a maximum of 2 children, up to ₹3,000 a month each. Farah receives ₹2,500 per child, which is within the limit, so ₹2,500 × 2 × 12 = ₹60,000 is exempt. The ₹30,000 paid for her third child is fully taxable.

body.title: Name the provision
body.textWithBlank: The section of the Income-tax Act, 2025 that sets out the new tax regime, and replaces Section 115BAC, is Section ___.
body.explanation: Section 202 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 replaces Section 115BAC of the 1961 Act. It lists which exemptions and deductions you give up when you stay in the default new regime.

body.title: Aarav asks HR for "tax-saving allowances"
body.scenario: Aarav hears that education allowance limits have jumped to ₹3,000 a month per child. He asks HR to move ₹72,000 of his special allowance into children education allowance and ₹40,000 into LTA, so that he can "save tax". He plans to stay in the new regime because he has no 80C investments or home loan.
body.prompt: Will this restructuring reduce Aarav's tax? What would you tell him?
body.modelAnswer: No. In the new regime, children education allowance and LTA are fully taxable, exactly like special allowance, so moving money between these labels changes nothing. The only way these allowances help is if he switches to the old regime, and that makes sense only if his total exemptions and deductions (HRA of ₹2,80,000, LTA, education allowance, Section 123 investments, health insurance and so on) are large enough to beat the new regime's lower rates and ₹75,000 standard deduction. In the new regime, the structuring moves that actually cut tax are employer NPS up to 14% of basic plus DA, meal vouchers within ₹200 per meal, and genuine official travel and conveyance reimbursements. He should ask HR about those instead.

Deducted from pay in many states, but reduces taxable salary only in the old regime.

body.title: Sort your own payslip
steps: List every earning component on your latest payslip
Mark each as fully taxable, partly exempt or not taxed
Cross out every old-regime-only exemption if you are in the new regime
Check meal vouchers stay within ₹200 per meal
Add up your exemptions and subtract the correct standard deduction for your regime
Compare your figure with the taxable salary in your Form 16 or your employer's tax projection

body.text: Limits are for tax year 2026-27 under the Income-tax Act, 2025 and the Income-tax Rules, 2026. Every exemption has conditions not fully covered here, and the following lessons go deeper into HRA, allowances and perquisites. This lesson is for education and is not personalised tax advice.

points: Every salary component is fully taxable, partly exempt or not taxed, and the answer can change with your regime.
Exemptions keep income out, deductions subtract after it is counted, and perquisites are valued by rules.
Basic, DA, special allowance, bonus, commission and in-service leave encashment are always fully taxable.
HRA, LTA and children education and hostel allowances help only in the old regime. The Rules, 2026 raised education allowance to ₹3,000 and hostel allowance to ₹9,000 a month per child.
Gratuity, retirement leave encashment, meal vouchers up to ₹200 per meal, official travel allowances and employer NPS still work in the new regime.
Professional tax reduces taxable salary only in the old regime.
